extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers (advanced high-school / undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and heuristic rules for proving inequalities, combinatorial statements, and induction-based results appearing in olympiad-style problem solving. Emphasis on when to apply induction variants and common inequality/transform tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Induction Principle (base case + inductive step; variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement f(n) ≥ g(n) for all n ∈ N, check a base case (often n=1 or n=0), assume the statement for n (or for all k < n in strong induction), and deduce it for n+1. Variants include starting at some n0 > 1, strong induction (assume for all k < n), and reverse induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify the appropriate base case(s). Choose ordinary or strong induction depending on whether the n+1 step requires only f(n) or all previous cases. The text notes equivalence with the well-ordering axiom and that many proofs use induction in nonstandard ways (e.g., reducing variables). Several examples illustrate building recursive proofs, reverse induction, and induction on composite parameters (like m+n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear denominators and treat sign/case splits in rational inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When expressions contain rational terms that might be negative, clear denominators before applying usual estimates and consider separate sign/case distinctions (e.g., x>y vs y>x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that some terms can be negative which complicates estimates unless denominators are cleared. After clearing denominators, treat the resulting polynomial/inequality in the appropriate sign-case(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminant arguments for quadratic-type inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when an expression is the discriminant of a quadratic (or can be arranged as such); show sign changes of the quadratic at sample points to infer positivity of the discriminant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: construct f(x)=a^2(a−2)x^2 − (a^3 − a + 2)x + (a^2+1) and compute f(0)>0, f(1)<0 to conclude positive discriminant, which yields the desired inequality. Checking signs at convenient points can be an efficient path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize/symmetry and use function complements + continuity to bound cyclic sums
rubrics_metrics.description: For cyclic rational sums like f(x,y,z)=x/(x+y)+y/(y+z)+z/(z+x), use normalization (divide by x+y+z), exploit identities/symmetries (e.g., f(x,y,z)=3−f(y,x,z)), and continuity to determine exact attainable range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show lower and upper bounds via simple comparisons (e.g., each term > x/(x+y+z)) and symmetry arguments; then use parametrized families (e.g., (x,tx,t^2x)) and take limits to show bounds are tight and the continuous range is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent half-angle substitution for trigonometric inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Set x = tan(α/2), y = tan(β/2), z = tan(γ/2) to convert trigonometric inequalities into algebraic ones; when α+β+γ = π this substitution is especially convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After substitution, assume the variables correspond to triangle angles; apply the Sine Law, area formulas, and relations involving circumradius R and inradius r to transform sums of sin(·), cos(·), and sin2(·) into expressions in sides/radii, which are often easier to bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply standard inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz, AM–GM, Chebyshev, Rearrangement) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a classical inequality suited to the expression's structure (e.g., apply Cauchy–Schwarz to sums of fractions/squares, AM–GM for product-sum tradeoffs, Chebyshev or Rearrangement for similarly-ordered sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: apply Cauchy–Schwarz to √(x/(y+z))-type terms, use AM–GM to derive lower bounds from xyz = 1, and note that many contestants used Chebyshev; Rearrangement can give alternate proofs. Always check equality cases to guide choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric circle/median theorems to convert geometry inequalities to algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: In triangle/circle problems, use known relations (e.g., extension of medians meeting circumcircle and A1A2·AA2 = BA2·A2C yielding A1A2 = a^2/(4m_a)) to express geometric segments algebraically and plug into algebraic inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After substituting these algebraic expressions, apply algebraic inequalities (like bounds on m_a, sums) to obtain desired numeric bounds (e.g., sum ≤ 3D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limiting arguments and continuity to show extremal values are attainable
rubrics_metrics.description: When bounding a continuous function of positive variables, examine parameterized paths (e.g., t→0 or t→∞ along (x,tx,t^2x)) to find limiting values and conclude the continuous range is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the function is continuous on the domain of interest, compute limits along paths to get infimum/supremum candidates, and then conclude all intermediate values occur by continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce n-variable problems by pushing an extremal variable to a boundary and induct
rubrics_metrics.description: When minimizing/maximizing a function of n ordered variables, analyze derivative/signs to show the extremum occurs when one variable equals a neighbor (e.g., x_n = x_{n−1}), then reduce to an (n−1)-variable problem and apply induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: find minimum of f(x_n) on [x_{n−1}, ∞); show derivative positive so min at x_{n−1}; replace x_n by x_{n−1} and continue by induction. This is a standard reduction technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square inequalities properly and factor differences of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with inequalities of expressions whose squares are easier to factor, move terms to one side, square (carefully preserving direction/signs), factor differences of squares, and combine factors to deduce constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: squaring led to (a−c−b)^2(b−c−a)^2(c−a−b)^2 ≤ 0, and because each factor is a square (nonnegative) the conclusion follows (at least one factor must be zero). Ensure squaring doesn't introduce extraneous solutions by checking sign conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret algebraic forms via law of cosines to infer angle/side relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite expressions like a^2 + b^2 − ab as a^2 + b^2 − 2ab cos 60° to identify that a,b,c can be triangle sides with a specific angle (e.g., 60°), then deduce ordering relations among angles/sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to reduce inequality statements to simple monotonic/order relations (e.g., deduce (a−c)(b−c) ≤ 0 by comparing angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept large overestimates when proving weak/rough inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: For some 'weak' inequalities where only a coarse bound is required, it is acceptable to make huge overestimations to simplify the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that simple proofs are sometimes possible because huge overestimations suffice; use such bounding when exact tightness is not required and it simplifies induction/argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution (e.g., x = 1/a) to exploit symmetry or product constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform variables to simplify constraints (e.g., xyz = 1) or symmetrise the expression; substitutions can convert complicated rational sums into forms amenable to CS or AM–GM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: setting x=1/a, y=1/b, z=1/c transforms sin-sum inequalities into sums of x^2/(y+z) with xyz=1, then apply Cauchy–Schwarz and AM–GM to deduce bounds and equality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use matrix algebra or Binet's formula for Fibonacci identities
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed-form expressions and divisibility/recurrence properties of Fibonacci numbers, use Binet's formula or matrix multiplication representations to derive identities and formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives several Fibonacci identities (Binet, multiplicative relations, gcd properties) and remarks that matrix multiplication helps in proofs; use these when direct combinatorial induction is cumbersome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloring-by-parity and recoloring arguments for planar division/map coloring
rubrics_metrics.description: Color regions by parity of containment (number of circles containing the region) or use recoloring (flip colors inside a newly added circle) to construct proper 2-colorings for regions generated by circles/lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods: (1) parity labeling gives immediate two-coloring; (2) induction with recoloring inside an added circle: outside keep colors, inside swap colors—neighbors across the circle have opposite colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pigeonhole principle (box principle) in combinatorial selection proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition collections (e.g., sums modulo n, groups of selected integers) and apply the pigeonhole principle to force equal remainders or desired divisibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: selecting n integers from 2n−1 integers to achieve divisibility by n uses partitioning and comparing remainders; similarly used in induction steps where multiple constructed sums produce repeated residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove uniqueness by induction with size/upper-bound arguments (Zeckendorf-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness of representations (e.g., Zeckendorf representation with nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers), use induction plus bounds to force the largest allowable term to appear and to rule out the next-larger term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that if N ≤ F_{n+1} and > F_n, then the representation must include F_n; use induction on the remainder N−F_n and bounds ensuring no forbidden adjacent terms are used. This method also proves uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extremal/erasure arguments in graph/map induction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In map/graph combinatorial proofs, remove an extremal object (a vertex, an edge, a closed path) whose removal preserves the required property, apply induction to the smaller structure, then reinsert the removed part with a controlled recoloring/counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remove a closed path in a graph to apply induction for proper coloring; remove two vertices and incident edges in triangle-free graphs to apply induction on edge counts. Carefully account for changes when reinserting.
